readings.title: Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
body: America, Actually Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026? ﻿Angie Nixon explains her playbook to be Florida’s next senator. by Cameron Peters and Astead Herndon Sep 6, 2026, 10:00 AM UTC Gift Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon visits Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood as she campaigns on August 29, 2026. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere. But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change. Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state , and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel . Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise? It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch. This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country. How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida? It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for. Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not. We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that. Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money. Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida. I wanted to ask about electability. Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism? The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1. I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people. We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary. They also volunteer in our campaign. They’ve made donations. We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense. They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message. Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million. She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities. People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires. People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people. In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2. And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus. The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism. Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years. T here’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza. Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats? I would say yes. I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk. But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby. You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel. Is that something you support? It is. I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community. So I’m fully supportive of that. You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website. It says that you support demilitarizing the police. And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.” What is the difference between that and defunding? Whatever folks think the difference is. I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words. But doesn’t that sound a little bit like lessening the resources that go to police to focus on other things? I mean, that sounds a little like the same thing. It sounds like I know that is my position. I want to defund Flock cameras because bad cops are stalking their ex-girlfriends and ex-boyfriends. And so to-may-toe, to-mah-toe. I literally said this before and that is what I am for. I’m not trying to get clipped in any kind of way. Let me ask you this way. I appreciate the focus on root causes, and I think you’ve laid that out that that’s where you want the energy to go — that real public safety comes from focusing on the things that cause people to commit crimes in the first place, but those often take a long time to show effect. If we’re talking about the root causes of crime, what is the message to someone whose community is unsafe right now that does not include policing? What I would say is, making sure that we invest in making sure people have more jobs and we invest in community control of the police. I totally believe in civil review boards and that type of thing, but I believe in making sure that people’s most basic needs are met. One of the things that I believe could help that right off the bat is things like universal healthcare, or at a minimum, extending the ACA subsidies so that we can drive down these healthcare premium costs. Or fully funding these programs that allow people to have access to first-time homebuyer programs. I was a single mom for 12 years, and I took part in the first-time homebuyer program that was funded from the federal government. That trickled down to the state and then to the local government. That helped me with down payment assistance as well as closing costs and those types of programs. We need to put policies in place that are allowing people to be good. We need to push for universal child care. For every $1 that is invested by the government, it puts $3 back into the economy so parents can get to work. They can be able to make sure that they have money to put their children in different programs. We need to invest in programs to keep our children off the streets. There’s been so much effort to put you in one of the boxes that have defined the Democratic ideological battles — DSA versus establishment. I hear in this interview how that doesn’t neatly fit with what it seems like you’ve done in Florida. Where do you think this campaign fits into the ongoing question of where do Democrats go next? We’re coalition builders, we’re aggregators. Folks should know, I was a vice chair of a local Democratic Party. I was also the field director and the political director with the state party. I have never fit in a box. I was a union member and I also led a statewide organization that was straight-up progressive. We need all these things to fight back against this Donald Trump regime. Look, this man is not going to leave willingly in 2028. He’s created a paramilitary force in the form of ICE that is getting away with shooting people and slaughtering them on camera while they’re masked without any accountability. They’re pushing to see how far they can go. Granted, Black people have been getting slaughtered on camera without accountability for a while, but now they are doing it to people who aren’t just Black, who aren’t just Latino. They are banking on us being normalized with what’s happening. First lady Michelle Obama says, “They go low, we go high.” I’m saying, “We get loud, we push back. We organize stronger and harder so that we can win and change this country and build a new vision for the next 250 years, where we have a Florida and an America for all.” See More : America, Actually Midterm Elections 2026 Podcasts Politics Video Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword The biggest advocate for slaughtering America’s wild horses might surprise you An evangelical explains what people get wrong about her faith A guy made a deepfake app to turn photos of women into nudes. ##段落
美国，实际上  
民主党能否在2026年翻转佛罗里达？安吉·尼克松解释了她在佛罗里达竞选参议员的策略。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯和阿斯特德·赫恩登，2026年9月6日，上午10:00 UTC  
赠品：民主党参议员候选人安吉·尼克松于2026年8月29日在迈阿密小哈瓦那社区竞选时亮相。乔·雷德尔/盖蒂图片社  
上个月，佛罗里达州众议员安吉·尼克松在民主党参议员提名中爆冷获胜，击败了资金更雄厚的对手、退役陆军中校亚历克斯·文德曼。她的胜利迅速被纳入民主党激进进步运动的叙事中，该运动已在密歇根、科罗拉多、纽约等地的众议院和参议院初选中获胜。但尽管尼克松支持进步政策，她认为故事远不止简单的进步派与中间派之争。她说她比对手更努力、组织更到位——而且佛罗里达各政治派别的人都在渴望改变。Vox的阿斯特德·赫恩登邀请尼克松参加一期特别的《美国，实际上》播客节目，解析她如何赢得提名、为什么她认为在这个许多分析人士认为是坚定红州的地方存在胜利之路，以及如果她在11月胜出，她作为参议员想实现什么目标。以下是他们对话的摘录，为简洁和清晰起见已做编辑。完整节目还有更多内容，所以请在您收听播客的任何平台收听《美国，实际上》，或在Vox的YouTube频道观看。  
您为什么认为您的胜利让这么多人感到意外？  
这让很多人感到意外，因为人们往往低估黑人女性——尤其是政治中进步的黑人女性——也低估那些筹款能力不足的人。但作为一位当了12年单亲妈妈的人，我知道怎么让一分钱掰成两半花。这场胜利归功于老式的草根组织工作。我曾是工会组织者，也是社区组织者，我深知人民力量的重要性，知道与人交谈、激发他们对为何投票、为何在这个国家看到自己身影的热情有多关键。  
您将这场胜利在多大程度上归因于您所描述的这种政治风格，而非您倡导的进步政策？我们是否应将此视为全民医保和“废除ICE”在佛罗里达有强力支持的信号？  
这全是综合因素，对吧？是我们在这场竞选中付出的辛勤努力，来提高人们对我是谁、我所坚持的政策和立场的认识，而这些政策和立场是大多数勤劳的普通民众所支持的。仅仅因为我们想要优质的医疗保健、可负担的住房和资金充足的公立学校，他们就试图散布恐惧，让我们看起来像是共产主义者，但我们不是。我们不是共产主义者。

我们是一群希望让勤奋工作的普通人掌握权力的人，以便他们能够决定和塑造我们的社区面貌以及我们的经济形态。这并不激进或极端。民主党人仍然认为你没有机会赢得大选。知名评论员曾表示，民主党不应在佛罗里达州投入资源，那将是浪费金钱。政治预测机构在你初选胜利后将选情转向有利于共和党的方向，声称进步政治使共和党更容易在佛罗里达这样的州获胜。我想问关于可当选性的问题。你能说明，在如此多的质疑声中，你如何能赢得全州范围的竞选吗？就像我能在初选中以1比18的经费劣势获胜一样。我正在建立一个非常独特、多元化的联盟。初选中，有共和党人和独立人士跨界投票支持我。他们还为我们的竞选做志愿者、捐款。我们确实有一群共和党人和自由意志主义者公开表示他们会投票给我，因为他们喜欢我不废话的风格。他们欣赏我试图制约来自华盛顿的残忍和腐败行为，这就是制胜的信息。看，我们面对的是一个允许1000万美元被盗的女性——现任共和党参议员阿什利·穆迪。她允许本应用于医疗需求和低收入儿童的资金被挪用，转向两个公民发起的投票倡议，而这些倡议实际上并没有改善我们社区的健康状况。人们感到沮丧，而阿什利·穆迪所做的一切就是只顾自己、她的竞选捐助者和那些亿万富翁。人民已经准备好让民选官员停止救助这些大企业，真正关心普通人。2023年11月，你在佛罗里达州众议院提出了一项决议，呼吁“在以色列和被占领的巴勒斯坦地区立即降级和停火”。该决议以104比2被否决，这也让你与佛罗里达州犹太核心小组的一些成员结下梁子。主席甚至称该决议源于无知和反犹主义。显然，民主党基础选民在过去几年中对这一问题的立场已发生变化。关于乔·拜登和卡玛拉·哈里斯在2024年大选中因没有更明确地与以色列在加沙的行动切割而损害自身利益，已有公开讨论。你认为这对民主党来说是一个错误吗？我会说是的。我认为我们必须在不同社区之间进行非常不舒服的对话，我们只需要坦诚交流。但我觉得，他们在处理这个问题上确实做得不够好。

##段落

与AIPAC游说团体一起。你曾提到此刻不支持向以色列提供任何资金或武器，但我也想问问关于BDS——即抵制、撤资或制裁以色列的运动——你是否支持？是的，我支持。我是一个黑皮肤女性，是奴隶的后代，也是民权运动人士的后代，我知道我们如何利用抵制和抗议为我们的社区赢得民权。所以我完全支持这一点。你反复表示不支持削减警察经费，你的网站上写着支持警察非军事化，并说“真正的安全来自好工作、优质学校、可负担住房和全民医疗——而非更多摄像头、更多牢笼和更多特工。”这与削减经费有何区别？不管别人觉得有什么区别。我不想把自己框死，因为我明白他们会如何利用我说某些词来剪辑和断章取义。但这听起来难道不有点像是减少投入警察的资源而转向其他方面吗？我的意思是，这听起来有点像同一回事。听起来——我知道这就是我的立场。我想削减Flock摄像头的经费，因为坏警察在跟踪他们的前女友和前男友。所以番茄、土豆，怎么说都行。我之前确实说过这话，这就是我所支持的。我不想以任何方式被剪辑。让我换个方式问。我理解你对根源问题的关注，我认为你也表明了那是你想投入精力的方向——真正的公共安全来自关注那些首先导致人们犯罪的因素，但这些往往需要很长时间才能见效。如果我们谈论犯罪的根源，对那些社区目前不安全的人，不包括警务在内的信息是什么？我要说的是，确保我们投资于让人们有更多工作，并投资于社区对警察的控制。我完全相信公民审查委员会这类机制，但我也相信要确保人们最基本的需求得到满足。我认为能立即有所帮助的事情之一包括全民医疗，或至少延长《平价医疗法案》的补贴，以便我们降低医保保费成本。或者全额资助那些让人们能获得首次购房者计划的项目。我曾是12年的单身母亲，参与了由联邦政府资助的首次购房者计划。资金从联邦流向州，再到地方政府。那帮助我获得了首付援助和过户费用等项目的支持。我们需要把警察——

目前已有一些机制在帮助人们向好发展。我们需要推动普及儿童照护服务。政府每投入1美元，经济就能回流3美元，这样父母才能去工作，确保有资金让孩子参加各类项目。我们需要投资于项目，防止孩子流落街头。  
##段落  
有那么多努力试图把你归入定义民主党意识形态斗争的某个阵营——民主社会主义者党团对建制派。我在这次采访中听到，这与你在佛罗里达所做的一切似乎并不完全吻合。你认为这次竞选在民主党未来走向的持续讨论中处于什么位置？  
我们是联盟建设者，是整合者。大家应该知道，我曾是地方民主党副主席，也曾担任州党部的现场主任和政治主任。我从不属于任何框框。我曾是工会成员，也领导过一个纯进步派的州级组织。我们需要所有这些力量来对抗唐纳德·特朗普政权。  
##段落  
看，这个人不会在2028年自愿离开。他以ICE的形式建立了一支准军事力量，他们在蒙面情况下枪杀和屠杀人们，摄像记录在案却无人问责。他们在试探能走多远。诚然，黑人长期以来在镜头下被屠杀却无人问责，但现在他们针对的不仅仅是黑人或拉丁裔。他们指望我们对正在发生的事情习以为常。  
##段落  
第一夫人米歇尔·奥巴马说：“他们走低路，我们走高路。”我说：“我们大声疾呼，我们反击。我们更强势、更努力地组织起来，以便赢得胜利，改变这个国家，为未来250年构建新愿景，让我们拥有一个面向所有人的佛罗里达和美国。”

readings.title: The retro tool for stranded astronauts
body: 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sophie Hardach An old seafaring instrument could help astronauts on ever more far-flung and perilous missions. Imagine you're an astronaut flying to Mars. Suddenly, disaster strikes: all your electronic navigation systems fail. How do you find your way back home? For Nasa astronauts, the answer could be a wayfinding tool invented around 300 years ago: the sextant . Used by seafarers on Earth, and astronauts on early Nasa missions, sextants are a last-resort navigation option for missions to the Moon, and potentially, beyond – in case the high-tech ones fail. Traditionally, sextants are used to measure the angle between celestial bodies such as stars and planets, to calculate one's own position. Apart from emergency use, these ancient star-sighting skills are also attracting increased interest from Nasa engineers as humans plan to venture to Mars and beyond. "The further and further we go out, the less and less we can rely on some of the Earth-based navigation technology," such as satellites, says Greg Holt, the navigation system manager for the Orion Spacecraft and its Artemis missions to the Moon. "And so you now have to fall back more and more on what I would call the classical navigation techniques. And some of those now harken back to the way navigation was done way back in the 16th, 17th, 18th Centuries," he explains.  In that age of classical navigation, "you actually had to look at the stars to figure out where you were, and figure out your orientation relative to those celestial bodies," he says. These are skills that can be crucial in deep space "because those are some of the only references you have once you get far away from Earth". In addition, knowing how to navigate by the stars can save lives, he points out: "We want to make sure that [the astronauts] have a way to safely navigate their way back home, if for some reason they lose communication with the Earth". In 2018, Holt and his team asked two astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS), Serena Auñón-Chancellor and Alexander Gerst, to test a hand-held sextant, taking measurements with the naked eye and a steady hand. "We had crew members demonstrate the use of a manual sextant, as an emergency means of back-up navigation to get the crew home from the Moon, if they had in fact lost communication," says Holt. "Because if you lose communication, you also lose that radio navigation link with the Earth, and you're on your own at that point." The experiment tapped deep into navigational history. In the 1960s, Nasa adapted ancient star-sighting methods to space flight, though initially astronauts were not entirely sure this would work. Neil Armstrong , the first man on the Moon, recalled that "one of the things that I was concerned with at the time was whether our navigation was sufficiently accurate [...] if we lost communication with Earth, for whatever reason, could we navigate by ourselves using celestial navigation? We thought we could, but these were undemonstrated skills." The answer was yes – he and other astronauts on those early flights did successfully use sextants and other naked-eye sighting methods, both routinely, and during emergencies. Buzz Aldrin resorted to a hand-held sextant and chart during the Gemini XII spaceflight in 1966, due to a problem with the radar. And during the near-disastrous Apollo 13 flight in 1970, Jim Lovell famously used the sight of the Earth on the last stretch to get home. During the Artemis II mission to the Moon, a hand-held emergency sextant like the one Holt demonstrated was kept ready during pre-launch The 2018 experiment with the sextant on the ISS was also successful. The results were accurate enough to suggest that navigating by hand-held sextant could get the crew back home in an emergency. And the astronauts reported that they found the sextant comfortable to use in microgravity – more so than using it on Earth, in fact. Speaking by video call from Houston, Holt holds up a black sextant – essentially, the same age-old tool used by seafarers, with some small modifications for space. Its edges have been rounded off, for example, to prevent it accidentally scraping something. And it has a hook-and-loop fastener to attach it to the wall of the spacecraft, and prevent it from floating around in microgravity. Other than that, it's exactly the same device you'd find on board a normal ship on an Earthly ocean, Holt says. On the Orion spacecraft, astronauts use a high-tech version of a sextant – an optical navigation system – as a first back-up if other navigation systems fail. A camera attached to the spacecraft takes images of the surrounding stars and planets, "doing all of the same things that a crew member would be doing with the sextant", Holt says. Using image-processing techniques, the camera takes measurements such as the angles between stars, the angles between stars and planets, and the diameter of a planet. The readings are then used to automatically calculate course-corrections, for example. "On the Orion spacecraft, the Optical Navigation system serves as a back-up, providing onboard navigation capability if communication and ground-based navigation support from Earth is lost," says Holt. During the Artemis missions, the system is routinely activated about once per day. "This allows us to confirm the system remains working and healthy, [to] collect valuable imagery and performance data for our engineering design team," he says. It is also "a cross-check confirmation of the navigation solution from the Earth-based tracking".  But if this high-tech system fails, the hand-held sextant comes in.  During the Artemis II mission to the Moon in April, a hand-held emergency sextant like the one Holt demonstrated was kept ready during pre-launch, he says. If there had been a problem with the cameras of the high-tech system at that point, the sextant would have been put on board at the last minute. It is not routinely packed on Orion, as it's not necessary equipment: "Every gram of mass counts when flying space missions," he points out.  If a disastrous systems failure happens after the launch, in space, the astronauts therefore won't have that hand-held sextant on board. But they are trained to know other naked-eye methods, Holt explains. One is to look for timings of when specific stars disappear behind the Earth, or the Moon, as a rough indicator of one's own position. To me, part of the fascination of my job is seeing how all of these techniques are all interrelated – Greg Holt Holt says familiarity with the original tool is useful for Nasa's engineers, too. When leading the teams that develop the high-tech systems, "I make sure they all go out and practice with a sextant so they understand basics where all this is coming from, the maths and geometry," he says. There are also other timeless navigational tricks that help modern-day astronauts. For example, the bright, easily recognisable stars and constellations that have historically guided seafarers, are also useful navigational points for astronauts in space, says Holt. That's because they are easy to spot and recognise by humans – whether those humans are on Earth, or in a spacecraft. More like this: • What happens when astronauts get stuck in space • Should astronauts abandon the ISS? • The switch that saved a Moon mission For Mars missions, those navigational points may include asteroids, Holt says. "We would say [to the astronaut], we expect that the asteroid is going to be half-way between the two head stars in Gemini , so look over there, find that asteroid between those two stars, take your readings, then compare that against the expectations and do the maths." If the readings are off, the astronauts correct the course to get to where they want to be. "To me, part of the fascination of my job is seeing how all of these techniques are all interrelated, from the earliest forms of star sightings off ships, all the way to how we're looking to navigate off to Mars and even further places," says Holt. Even the most far-flung missions still involve the same fundamental concepts, he says: looking at stars, looking at objects in comparison to the stars, and using geometric relationships to determine where we are. "Whether we are doing it manually with a stick, or a sextant, or a high-tech camera, it's fascinating to me that a lot of these same techniques are all linked and have those common heritages and mathematical foundations." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.    For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 三天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 索菲·哈达克 一种古老的航海仪器可能帮助宇航员执行日益遥远和危险的 missions。想象你是一名飞往火星的宇航员。突然，灾难降临：你所有的电子导航系统都失效了。你如何找到回家的路？对于NASA宇航员来说，答案可能是一种约300年前发明的寻路工具：六分仪。六分仪曾被地球上的海员和早期NASA任务的宇航员使用，是前往月球乃至更远任务中的最后备用导航选项，以防高科技系统失灵。传统上，六分仪用于测量星星和行星等天体之间的角度，以计算自身位置。除了紧急用途外，随着人类计划向火星及更远地方进发，这些古老的观星技能也日益引起NASA工程师的兴趣。

##段落  
“我们走得越远，就越少能依赖一些基于地球的导航技术，”例如卫星，猎户座飞船及其阿尔忒弥斯登月任务的导航系统经理格雷格·霍尔特说。“所以你现在不得不越来越多地依赖我所说的经典导航技术。其中一些现在可以追溯到16、17、18世纪的导航方式，”他解释说。在那个经典导航时代，“你实际上必须观察星星来确定你在哪里，并确定你相对于那些天体的方向，”他说。这些技能在深空中可能至关重要，“因为一旦你远离地球，这些就是你仅有的参考之一”。此外，知道如何通过星星导航可以挽救生命，他指出：“我们想确保（宇航员）有一种方法能安全导航回家，如果他们因某种原因失去与地球的通信”。2018年，霍尔特和他的团队要求国际空间站上的两名宇航员塞雷娜·奥尼翁-钱塞勒和亚历山大·格斯特测试手持六分仪，用肉眼和稳定的手进行测量。

##段落  
“我们让机组人员演示了手动六分仪的使用，作为应急备用导航手段，以便如果他们真的失去通信，能从月球返回地球，”霍尔特说。“因为如果你失去通信，你也失去了与地球的无线电导航连接，那时你就只能靠自己了。”这项实验深入挖掘了导航历史。在20世纪60年代，NASA将古老的观星方法适应于太空飞行，尽管最初宇航员并不完全确定这能否奏效。第一个登上月球的人尼尔·阿姆斯特朗回忆说，“我担心的事情之一……”

当时的问题是，我们的导航是否足够精确[...]如果出于任何原因我们与地球失去通信，我们能否依靠自己使用天体导航来定位？我们相信可以，但这些都是未经证实的技能。"答案是肯定的——他和早期飞行中的其他宇航员确实成功使用了六分仪和其他裸眼观测方法，既在常规操作中，也在紧急情况下使用。巴兹·奥尔德林在1966年的双子座十二号太空飞行中，由于雷达出现问题，不得不使用手持六分仪和星图。而在1970年险些酿成大祸的阿波罗十三号飞行中，吉姆·洛弗尔在最后返航阶段著名地利用了对地球的目视观测。在阿尔忒弥斯二号登月任务中，像霍尔特演示的那种手持应急六分仪在发射前一直备好待用。2018年在国际空间站上进行的六分仪实验也取得了成功。其结果足够精确，表明在紧急情况下，使用手持六分仪导航可以让机组人员返回地球。而且宇航员们报告说，他们发现在微重力环境下使用六分仪很舒适——实际上比在地球上使用还要舒适。霍尔特通过视频通话从休斯顿讲话，举起一个黑色六分仪——本质上，这是水手们使用的古老工具，只是为太空做了一些小改动。例如，它的边缘已被磨圆，以防止意外刮擦到其他物体。它还有一个钩环扣件，用于固定在航天器壁上，防止它在微重力中飘浮。除此之外，它和普通船只在地球海洋上使用的装置完全相同，霍尔特说。在猎户座航天器上，宇航员使用一种高科技版本的六分仪——光学导航系统——作为其他导航系统失效时的第一备用方案。安装在航天器上的摄像机会拍摄周围恒星和行星的图像，"执行宇航员用六分仪所做的所有相同操作"，霍尔特说。利用图像处理技术，摄像机会测量诸如恒星之间的角度、恒星与行星之间的角度以及行星直径等数据。然后，这些读数会被用于自动计算航向修正，例如。"在猎户座航天器上，光学导航系统作为备用方案，如果与地球的通信和地面导航支持中断，它提供机载导航能力，"霍尔特说。在阿尔忒弥斯任务期间，该系统大约每天例行启动一次。"这让我们能够确认系统保持运行和健康状态，[并]为我们的工程设计团队收集宝贵的图像和性能数据，"他说。它也是对来自地面跟踪的导航解决方案的"交叉验证确认"。

但如果这一高科技系统失灵，手持六分仪便会派上用场。霍尔特表示，在4月执行阿尔忒弥斯二号月球任务期间，一台类似他演示的手持应急六分仪在发射前一直处于待命状态。若当时高科技系统的摄像头出现问题，六分仪将在最后一刻被装上飞船。它并非猎户座飞船的常规配备，因为并非必需设备，他指出：“执行太空任务时，每一克质量都至关重要。”因此，如果发射后在太空中发生灾难性系统故障，宇航员手边不会有这台手持六分仪。但霍尔特解释说，他们接受过训练，掌握其他裸眼观测方法。其中一种方法是观察特定恒星消失在地球或月球背后的时间，以此粗略判断自身位置。对我而言，工作的魅力之一在于看到所有这些技术如何相互关联——格雷格·霍尔特。霍尔特还表示，熟悉原始工具对美国宇航局的工程师们同样有用。在领导开发高科技系统的团队时，“我确保他们都出去用六分仪实践，以便理解其中的基本原理、数学和几何学，”他说。还有其他永恒不变的导航技巧也能帮助现代宇航员。例如，历史上指引航海者的明亮且易于识别的恒星和星座，对太空中的宇航员也是有用的导航参考点，霍尔特说。这是因为它们容易被人类发现和辨认——无论这些人类身处地球还是航天器内。更多类似内容：• 宇航员被困太空时会发生什么 • 宇航员应否放弃国际空间站？ • 拯救登月任务的开关。对于火星任务，这些导航点可能包括小行星，霍尔特说。“我们会[对宇航员]说，我们预计这颗小行星将位于双子座两颗主星之间，所以看向那边，找到那颗位于两星之间的小行星，进行读数，然后与预期对比并计算。”如果读数有偏差，宇航员便修正航线以到达目的地。“对我而言，工作的魅力之一在于看到所有这些技术如何相互关联，从船上最早的观星形式，一直到我们探索火星乃至更远地方的导航方式，”霍尔特说。即使是距离最远的任务，也仍涉及相同的基本概念，他说：观察恒星，将物体与恒星对比，并利用几何关系确定我们的位置。“无论是用木棍、六分仪，还是高科技摄像头手动操作，我都觉得这很奇妙。”

很多这些相同技术都是相互关联的，并拥有共同的传统和数学基础。”——如果你喜欢这个故事，欢迎订阅《要闻清单》新闻简报——每周两次精选特稿、视频和不容错过的新闻，直接发送至你的邮箱。如需获取BBC更多科学、技术、环境和健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。太空 宇航员 太阳系 科学 天文学 火星 月球 技术 数学 特稿

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

##段落
觉得老板没看见你的努力？你可以这样做  
2023年6月15日  
/  
海莉·考德威尔  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
Stocksy

##段落
你有没有过这样的经历：你的辛勤工作——包括你的成功——被经理完全忽视？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而来——帮助那些带着职场烦恼来电的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西丝·弗莱和安妮·莫里斯认识了来电者奈阿。在一次大规模重组后，她被分配到了一位新上司手下，而这位上司忙于事务，让她难以获得认可。奈阿尽心尽力想把工作做好，但缺乏肯定、鼓励——甚至是对她工作的基本关注——让她逐渐失去了动力。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情中的人性——以及你经理的人性。

##段落
“有时，阻碍你与经理成为优秀合作伙伴的，可能是你对现状还残留着一些挫败感，”安妮解释道。“但那种情绪对你不会有帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿去看到经理身上的人性，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮还分享了这样一条策略让她实践：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西丝是这样说的：“你在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。所以如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼数职的人时，我们该如何为他们创造成功的条件？”

##段落
“好奇心的最简单表达——它确实是职场中的神奇灵药——就是提问的形式，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问经理，什么流程最适合他们了解你的成就和贡献。或者，你可以专注于如何让与他们的会议更高效，问他们：“我们的一对一时间怎样才能为我们共同想要实现的目标服务？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚地表达你的担忧，并询问经理他们对你成功的愿景是什么样子的。你可以这样说：“我的担心是：我工作非常努力，在这种变动不定的状态下，我怕六个月过去了，大家会怀疑我到底有没有做好工作。所以对我来说，明确一下很有帮助——什么是‘做好工作’，我能怎样帮你获取那些评估数据？”

##段落
在全世界各个行业，许多人正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，面对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，需要一段重新调整的时期，这都很正常。

##段落
带着问题去沟通——并把老板视为与你协作的另一个普通人——能帮你重新找回一些主动权和自主感。

##段落
“试着做你力所能及的事，然后惊奇地观察对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一张你希望对方如何改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我想你会惊喜的；这正是这件事的美妙之处。”

##段落
无论你从事什么工作或经营什么业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到改善工作日的实用建议。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩大你的副业项目，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击此处，有机会在节目中提出你自己的职场问题并获得解答！现在就在你收听播客的任何平台上收听《Fixable》。

readings.title: Is New York's cannabis business flying high?
body: 26 March 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mike Wendling Five years after it was legalised in the state, cannabis is seemingly everywhere in New York. But, business owners say that many legitimate outlets are struggling – largely because of a thriving grey market, and the complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry. If you've recently visited New York, you've probably noticed something.  Advertisements outside bodegas display pictures of bright green flowers, higher-end dispensaries that resemble coffee bars or electronics shops welcome customers from all over the world, and then of course there's the smell – so seemingly omnipresent that even US Open tennis players have complained .  Weed is everywhere. From the outside it looks like a free-for-all, one that is drawing scepticism even from voices broadly supportive of the aims of the legalisation – including reducing harm and boosting tax revenue. Social media is rife with complaints (typical comments include "New York could not have screwed up legal weed any worse!") and for years the local press has been chronicling the rise of the "weed bodega" – typically a corner store selling products of dubious provenance. Across the country, weed consumption has increased – though studies indicate  that the rate of young people using has gradually declined since the turn of the century.  Things may have come to a head recently when the  New York Times , once a legal weed supporter, published an editorial headlined: "Marijuana Is Everywhere. That's a Problem." The newspaper now argues that "marijuana is causing more harm than predicted" and calls for tighter regulation.  But this new green rush is not as straightforward as it seems. Business owners say that public perceptions have been sullied by illegal operators, and that many above-board businesses are struggling – largely because of the incredibly complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry.  "At first glance, New York's cannabis industry appears to be booming," says Jayson Tantalo, a cannabis businessman and vice president of operations for the New York Cannabis Retail Association. "But that perception was initially driven by an oversaturation of illicit operators.  "These shops often presented themselves as legitimate, creating a misleading sense of scale and economic success," he says.  New York state legalised recreational use of cannabis five years ago this month . But legal wrangling and slow issuing of licenses hampered initial growth, while sales in other states such as California were racing ahead.   The bottleneck was so restrictive that some growers in New York complained that their crops were going to waste because of the lack of retail sales outlets. Meanwhile hundreds of those shady outlets sprang up, particularly in New York City.  Those wild days may be coming to an end. State authorities are starting to crack down on illegal operators, and police have been given power to immediately shut shops without a licence. And more legal businesses are being set up to address pent-up demand.  "It was really out of control," says Vlad Bautista, co-founder of Happy Munkey, a cannabis retailer in the Inwood neighbourhood of Manhattan.  "It made a little dent," he says of recent enforcement efforts. "But there’s still a long way to go." CRB Monitor, a firm that researches the cannabis industry, counts more than 2,000 active cannabis business licenses across the state – including retailers, wholesalers, growers and other types of cannabis companies – with another nearly 5,000 applications in the pipeline.  The effects can be seen far from Manhattan with weed shops popping up all across a state that is roughly the size of England.  Jayson Tantalo owns one of them. He was involved in the weed business long before it was legal. "What started as survival evolved into deep expertise in the industry," he says. He and his wife Britni set up their Flower City Dispensary retail business in Victor, a suburban community in western New York state with a population of about 16,000.  Tantalo says that while the industry is "highly visible and normalised" across the state, only a small percentage of legal operators have captured large shares of the market.  "Growth exists, but it's constrained, uneven, and still stabilising," he says.  New York's growing pains are just one example of the extraordinarily complicated legal status of cannabis that has caused confusion across the country - for businesses, customers and the public.  The patchwork legal regime around the industry is a product of cannabis's long strange trip from respectability to contraband and back again. George Washington, the first US president, famously grew hemp crops at his estate.   But waves of restrictions followed, culminating in a 1970 law that deemed marijuana a Schedule I drug – the most restrictive category.  Despite the US government's war on drugs, there has always been a significant movement calling for looser regulations on cannabis. That movement gradually became more mainstream in the early years of this century.  Support for legalising cannabis first cracked 50% of Americans in 2013, according to polling firm Gallup, and that figure has since risen to more than two-thirds today.  But instead of blanket legalisation, reforms came in piecemeal fashion, on the state and sometimes even the local level, creating a fragmented state-by-state market.  To top it off, weed remains illegal under federal law – thousands of people still get arrested each year for marijuana possession and related crimes.  This legal patchwork results in some bizarre consequences. A road-tripper heading west from New York would pass through Pennsylvania, where recreational use of marijuana is illegal, and then into Ohio, where it was legalised by a 2023 referendum. If they continued along Interstate 80 they would eventually get to Indiana (where weed is illegal), Illinois (legal), and Iowa (illegal) – and so on.  That's confusing in itself. But another legal loophole has opened the door for all sorts of grey-market and online businesses, effectively making cannabis accessible to nearly everyone in the country.  The 2018 Farm Bill legalised hemp with a relatively low level of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC – the chemical that gets cannabis users high.  Hemp contains CBD – a chemical that doesn’t produce the high of THC but has some health benefits. A glut of CBD ensued. And in a lab, CBD can be converted into psychoactive THC.  "Entrepreneurs could say, 'this is just hemp', even if what they were producing was a highly intoxicating form of THC," says Chris Lindsay, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH), which represents licenced businesses.  Those products are sold online or in those weed bodegas – even in states that have not legalised marijuana.  Robin Goldstein, an economist at the University of California-Davis and co-author of the book Can Legal Weed Win?: The Blunt Realities of Cannabis Economics, estimates that just behind California, the second-biggest weed market is in Texas, despite the Lone Star state's blanket ban on recreational cannabis use.  Business owners like Jason Ambrosino, have become used to dealing with spiralling legal complexities.  Ambrosino is founder and chief executive of Veterans Holdings, a weed business based in Gloversville, New York, about three hours north of New York City. An army vet who was seriously injured in Iraq, he got into the cannabis industry after discovering that medical marijuana was effective in alleviating his pain. These days, he says his legal headaches include rules that make it impossible to branch out into neighbouring states or to obtain traditional sources of financing.  "There’s a million different ways to get institutional funding, but you can’t get any of those for cannabis because of federal law," he says.  Despite the headwinds, Ambrosino has managed to grow his business and now employs around 80 people, and is hopeful that the increased licences for legal shops in New York will mean more sales opportunities down the line.  Vlad Bautista, the Happy Munkey co-founder, roughly estimates that he spends 40% of his time complying with various regulations, and, in particular, he questions some of the rules around advertising and tax law.  "If you own a cannabis business, you have much stricter advertising regulations than companies selling alcohol, cigarettes or gambling," he says. "You're stuck in the stone age, handing out flyers on the street." A buzz ran through the industry in December of last year, when President Trump signed an executive order which directed officials to accelerate efforts to reclassify marijuana to a less stringent category.  That might eventually give cannabis businesses some added profits – due to another federal law, weed companies aren't able to deduct all of their normal business expenses from their taxes. But businesspeople and experts aren't holding their breath for a practical impact any time soon.  "It's smoke and mirrors," says Naomi Granger, founder and chief executive of the National Association of Cannabis Accounting and Tax Professionals, who says some headlines heralding a new dawn for the cannabis industry have been somewhat misleading.  Some industry insiders say uncertainty is part and parcel of a nascent industry.  Steve Kemmerling, founder and chief executive of CRB Monitor, notes that states that were earlier to legal weed – California and Colorado in the western US were among the first – experienced hiccups on the way to relative stability.  "In any new market you're going to have wild volatility and price swings, mergers and acquisitions, along with competitive businesses and people cutting corners," he says.  And in a buzzy industry perhaps it's not surprising to encounter businesspeople who seem hard wired for sunny-day thinking.  "I'm an optimist," says Vlad Bautista. "We live in a divided and polarised world where nobody agrees on everything, and when you look at public opinion, there's a majority of people who agree on legal cannabis." "We've made a ton of progress," he says, "but there's still a long way to go." Please visit BBC Action Line for support with drug addiction. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn .   Business Drugs Features

2026年3月26日 分享 保存 设为谷歌偏好 麦克·温德林 在该州合法化五年后，大麻在纽约似乎无处不在。但企业主表示，许多合法门店正陷入困境——主要是因为灰色市场的繁荣，以及美国大麻产业复杂的法律地位。 如果你最近去过纽约，你可能会注意到一些事情。小杂货店外的广告展示着亮绿色花朵的图片，更高端的药房看起来像咖啡吧或电子商店，欢迎来自世界各地的顾客，当然还有那种气味——似乎无处不在，连美国网球公开赛的选手都抱怨过。大麻无处不在。从外表看，这像是一场无节制的狂欢，甚至引起了对合法化目标（包括减少危害和增加税收）总体持支持态度的人士的质疑。社交媒体上充斥着抱怨（典型评论包括“纽约不可能把合法大麻搞得更糟了！”），多年来，当地媒体一直在报道“大麻杂货店”的兴起——通常是指销售来源可疑产品的街角商店。全美范围内，大麻消费量有所增加——尽管研究表明，自世纪之交以来，年轻人的使用率逐渐下降。 事情可能最近达到了顶点，《纽约时报》——曾经是合法大麻的支持者——发表了一篇社论，标题为：“大麻无处不在。这是个问题。”该报现在认为，“大麻造成的危害比预期的更大”，并呼吁加强监管。 但这场新的绿色热潮并不像表面看起来那么简单。企业主表示，公众的看法已被非法经营者玷污，许多合规企业正在苦苦挣扎——主要是因为美国大麻产业极其复杂的法律地位。 “乍一看，纽约的大麻产业似乎在蓬勃发展，”大麻商人、纽约大麻零售协会运营副总裁杰森·坦塔洛说。“但这种看法最初是由非法经营者的过度饱和所驱动的。” “这些商店往往将自己伪装成合法的，造成了一种误导性的规模和经济效益感，”他说。 纽约州在本月迎来了娱乐用大麻合法化五周年。但法律纠纷和许可证发放缓慢阻碍了初期增长，而加利福尼亚等其他州的销售却一马当先。这种瓶颈极其严格，以至于纽约的一些种植者抱怨说，由于缺乏零售销售渠道，他们的作物正在浪费。与此同时，数百家那些可疑的店铺如雨后春笋般涌现，尤其是在

在纽约市。那些狂野的日子可能即将结束。州当局开始打击非法经营者，警方已被授权立即关闭无照商店。同时，更多合法企业正在设立，以满足被压抑的需求。“这真的失控了，”曼哈顿因伍德社区大麻零售商Happy Munkey的联合创始人弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。“这起了一点作用，”他谈到最近的执法努力时说，“但还有很长的路要走。”研究大麻行业的公司CRB Monitor统计，全州有超过2000个活跃的大麻商业许可证——包括零售商、批发商、种植者和其他类型的大麻公司——另有近5000份申请正在审批中。这种影响远不止曼哈顿，在这个面积与英格兰相当的大州，大麻店遍地开花。杰森·坦塔洛就是其中一家店的老板。他在大麻合法化之前很久就涉足这一行业。“起初是为生存而战，后来演变成对行业的深厚专长，”他说。他和妻子布丽特尼在纽约州西部维克托郊区社区（人口约16000）开设了他们的Flower City药房零售业务。坦塔洛表示，尽管该行业在全州“高度可见且已常态化”，但只有少数合法运营商占据了较大的市场份额。“增长存在，但受到限制、不均衡，且仍在稳定中，”他说。纽约的成长烦恼只是大麻极其复杂法律地位的一个例子，这种复杂性在全美范围内给企业、消费者和公众造成了混乱。围绕该行业的零散法律体系，是大麻从体面到违禁品再回归的漫长奇异旅程的产物。美国第一任总统乔治·华盛顿以其庄园种植大麻而闻名。但随后一波又一波的限制接踵而至，最终在1970年的一项法律中将大麻列为第一类管制药物——即限制最严格的类别。尽管美国政府开展了毒品战争，但一直有相当规模的运动呼吁放宽对大麻的管制。本世纪初，这场运动逐渐变得更加主流。根据民调公司盖洛普的数据，2013年支持大麻合法化的美国人首次突破50%，而如今这一数字已升至三分之二以上。但改革并非全面合法化，而是在州甚至地方层面零敲碎打地推进，形成了各州支离破碎的市场。更糟糕的是，大麻在联邦法律下仍然非法——每年仍有数千人因持有大麻及相关罪行被捕。这种法律拼凑状

混乱的工作状态导致了一些离奇的结果。一名从纽约向西出发的公路旅行者会经过宾夕法尼亚州，那里娱乐性大麻是非法的，然后进入俄亥俄州，那里在2023年通过公投将大麻合法化。如果他们继续沿80号州际公路行驶，最终会到达印第安纳州（大麻非法）、伊利诺伊州（合法）和爱荷华州（非法），如此反复。这本身就令人困惑。但另一个法律漏洞为各种灰色市场和在线业务打开了大门，实际上使全国几乎每个人都能接触到大麻。2018年的农业法案将四氢大麻酚（THC）含量相对较低的大麻合法化，THC是让大麻使用者兴奋的化学物质。大麻含有CBD——一种不会产生THC那种兴奋感但有一些健康益处的化学物质。随后CBD出现了过剩。在实验室里，CBD可以转化为具有精神活性的THC。“企业家可以说，‘这只是大麻’，即使他们生产的是高度致醉形式的THC，”代表持牌企业的美国大麻和大麻贸易协会政策与州倡导副总裁克里斯·林赛表示。这些产品在网上或那些大麻商店销售，即使在尚未将大麻合法化的州也是如此。加州大学戴维斯分校的经济学家罗宾·戈尔茨坦，也是《合法大麻能赢吗？：大麻经济的直白现实》一书的合著者，估计仅次于加利福尼亚州，第二大麻市场是德克萨斯州，尽管孤星州全面禁止娱乐性大麻使用。像杰森·安布罗西诺这样的企业主已经习惯了应对日益复杂的法律问题。安布罗西诺是总部位于纽约格洛弗斯维尔的大麻企业Veterans Holdings的创始人兼首席执行官，该地距离纽约市以北约三小时车程。他是一名在伊拉克受重伤的退伍军人，在发现医用大麻能有效缓解他的疼痛后进入了这个行业。他说，如今他的法律头痛包括规则使他无法扩展到邻近州或获得传统融资渠道。“有无数种方式可以获得机构资金，但由于联邦法律，你无法为大麻获得任何一种，”他说。尽管面临逆风，安布罗西诺还是设法扩大了他的业务，现在雇佣了大约80人，并希望纽约合法商店许可证的增加意味着未来会有更多销售机会。Happy Munkey联合创始人弗拉德·包蒂斯塔粗略估计，他花费40%的时间来遵守各种法规，特别是质疑一些关于广告和税法的规则。“如果你拥有一家大麻

##段落
他说：“比起销售酒精、香烟或赌博的公司，你的广告监管要严格得多。你还停留在石器时代，只能在街上发传单。”去年12月，特朗普总统签署了一项行政命令，指示官员加快将大麻重新归类到更宽松类别的进程，这一消息在业内引起了一阵轰动。由于另一项联邦法律，大麻公司无法从税收中扣除所有正常业务开支——这项命令最终可能会为大麻企业带来一些额外利润。但商界人士和专家并不指望短期内会有实际影响。全国大麻会计与税务专业人士协会创始人兼首席执行官娜奥米·格兰杰表示：“这不过是障眼法。”她说，一些预示大麻行业新黎明到来的头条新闻有些误导性。一些业内人士表示，不确定性是一个新兴行业不可避免的一部分。CRB Monitor创始人兼首席执行官史蒂夫·凯默林指出，较早合法化大麻的州——美国西部的加利福尼亚州和科罗拉多州便是首批——在走向相对稳定的过程中也经历了波折。他说：“在任何新市场中，你都会遇到剧烈的波动和价格起伏、并购交易，以及竞争激烈的企业和偷工减料的行为。”而在这个热闹非凡的行业里，遇到一些似乎天生乐观的生意人也许并不令人意外。弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说：“我是个乐观主义者。我们生活在一个分裂且两极分化的世界里，没有人能在所有事情上达成一致，但当你看看公众舆论，大多数人都认同大麻合法化。”他说：“我们已经取得了很大进展，但还有很长的路要走。”如需药物成瘾方面的帮助，请访问BBC Action Line。——如需面向董事会及更广泛领域的全球洞察和专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《必读清单》则会精选专题和见解。欲了解更多商业及更广泛领域的信息，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业毒品专题

readings.title: My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
body: Advice My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something. ﻿To save the humanities, we need to rethink our assumptions about AI — and education. by Sigal Samuel Updated Sep 6, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift Pete Gamlen for Vox Part Of The rapid development of AI has benefits — and poses serious risks see all updates Sigal Samuel is a correspondent for Vox’s Future Perfect. She writes primarily about the future of consciousness, tracking advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience and their staggering ethical implications. Before joining Vox, Sigal was the religion editor at the Atlantic. Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year. This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here . I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes. This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too. Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting. But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies. And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment. I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does. How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent? Dear Troubled Teacher, I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed! So: What is the real value of a humanities education? Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields. Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films. But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion. That’s never what they were supposed to be. Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes , is “the formation of human persons.” In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product. She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process. Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here! This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece. He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life. But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision. And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham. As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him , “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision. The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character. I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!” It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects. But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now. Your job is to be their Aristotle. For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis , or practical wisdom. And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI. Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot . It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you. Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie !). If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context. This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world. The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to. The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice. Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction . Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout. Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use. “Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it. And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.” So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing. If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy. Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit. Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without. Both are totally fine. But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process. I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using. As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it. Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it). All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have. So use every bit of it. Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation. You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite. If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them. But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion. At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim. None of this is easy. I feel for you and all other educators who are struggling in this confusing environment. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some educators are suffering from moral injury , a psychological condition that arises when you feel you’ve been forced to violate your own values. But maybe it can comfort you to remember that this is much bigger than you. Generative AI is an existential threat to a humanities education as currently constituted. Over the next few years, humanities departments will have to paradigm-shift or perish. If they want to survive, they’ll need to get brutally honest about their true mission. For now, from your pre-paradigm-shift perch, all you can do is make the choices that are left for you to make. I went back to Shannon Vallor’s first book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting . If there’s one book I could get everyone in the AI world to read, it would be this one. And I think it can be useful to everyone else, too, because we all need to cultivate what Vallor calls the “technomoral virtues” — the traits that will allow us to adapt well to emerging technologies. A New Yorker piece about AI and cognitive atrophy led me to a 2024 psychology paper titled “The Unpleasantness of Thinking: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Association Between Mental Effort and Negative Affect.” The authors’ conclusion: “We suggest that mental effort is inherently aversive.” Come again? Yes, sometimes I just want to turn off my brain and watch Netflix, but sometimes thinking about a challenging topic is so pleasurable! To me, it feels like running or weightlifting: Too much is exhausting, but the right amount is exhilarating. And what feels like “the right amount” can go up or down depending on how much I practice. Astrobiologist Sara Imari Walker published an essay in Noema provocatively titled “ AI Is Life .” She reminds us that evolution produced us and we produced AI. “It is therefore part of the same ancient lineage of information that emerged with the origin of life,” she writes. “Technology is not artificially replacing life — it is life.” To be clear, she’s not arguing that tech is alive; she’s saying it’s an outgrowth of human life, an extension of our own species. This story was originally published in The Highlight , Vox’s member-exclusive magazine. To get early access to member-exclusive stories every month, join the Vox Membership program today . 我的学生们认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们发现了什么。为了拯救人文学科，我们需要重新思考对AI——以及教育——的假设。作者：西格尔·塞缪尔 更新于2026年9月6日，UTC时间中午12:00 礼物 皮特·甘伦为Vox绘制 部分 AI的快速发展带来了好处——也带来了严重风险 查看所有更新 西格尔·塞缪尔是Vox“未来完美”栏目的记者。她主要撰写关于意识未来的文章，追踪人工智能和神经科学的进展及其令人震惊的伦理影响。加入Vox之前，西格尔是《大西洋月刊》的宗教编辑。编者按，9月6日东部时间上午8点：在西格尔·塞缪尔休产假期间，我们为您带来一些最受欢迎的“里程可能因人而异”专栏。以下这篇最初发表于去年。这期非传统建议专栏为您提供了一个独特的框架，用来思考道德困境。它基于价值多元主义：即我们每个人都拥有多种价值，这些价值同样有效，但常常相互冲突。在此提交您自己的问题。我是一名大学助教，负责大型人文学科讲座课程的讨论小组。这也意味着我要批改大量学生写作——而且，不可避免地，也会看到大量AI写作。当然，我们很多人都在努力设计作业和教学法，以降低这种诱惑。但作为助教，我实施这些政策的能力有限。与此同时，AI生成的写作如此普遍，以至于要认真对待课程政策，甚至把每一个疑似案例都上报给授课教授，那基本上每份作业都要提出几十次指控，其中一些还是误报。我相信人文学科教育具有神圣不可言喻的价值，但我也不会通过对每个人都在做的事情进行严厉打压，去说服那些压力重重的19岁学生相信这种价值。我该如何思考执行一个他们并不认真对待的机构的规则的伦理问题，或者为了营造一个不那么像需要绕过的障碍的课堂而放任自流？亲爱的烦恼的老师，我知道你说你相信“人文学科教育不可言喻的价值”，但如果我们想真正理清你的困境，那种不可言喻的价值必须被言说出来！那么：人文学科教育的真正价值是什么？放眼现代大学，人们可能会认为人文学科与STEM领域并无太大不同。正如工程系或数学系通过指出其创造的产品——桥梁设计、天气预报——来证明自身存在的合理性，如今的人文学科系也通过指出其学生同样创造产品来证明自身存在的合理性：文学解读。

##段落
翻译、文化批评、短片。但说真的：是大学的新自由主义化迫使人文科学陷入那种怪异的扭曲。那从来不是它们本该有的样子。正如哲学家梅根·弗里茨所写，它们的真正目标是“人的形成”。换句话说，虽然其他院系的目的最终是创造产品，但人文教育本该不同，因为学生本身就是产品。她才是学习过程中被创造和再创造的对象。填写这份匿名表格！订阅者将比其他人都更早看到我的专栏，他们的问题也会在未来的版本中被优先处理。在此注册！

##段落
这种教育愿景——作为一种旨在个人转变的追求——正是亚里士多德在古希腊时期提出的。他认为真正的目标不是传授知识，而是培养美德：诚实、正义、勇气，以及所有那些促成丰盈人生的性格特质。但由于在我们的超资本主义社会中，丰盈被贬低，你发现自己被困在最初的愿景和如今基于产品、功利主义的愿景之间。而学生们——正确地！——感觉到生成式AI证明了人文科学的功利主义愿景是个骗局。正如一位学生对他在纽约大学的教授所说，为了证明用AI帮他做作业的合理性：“你让我从A点到B点，我为什么不用车去呢？”这是一个完全合乎逻辑的论点——只要你接受功利主义的愿景。那么，真正的解决方案是对人文科学的目的保持诚实：你的事业是帮助学生培养他们的品格。我知道，我知道：很多学生会说：“我没时间培养品格！我只需要找到工作！”他们专注于就业前景完全合理。但你的工作是专注于别的东西——一些能帮助他们在长远中丰盈的东西，即使他们现在不完全看到它的价值。你的工作就是做他们的亚里士多德。

##段落
对于这位古希腊哲学家来说，所有美德之母是phronesis，即实践智慧。而我想说，你能为学生做的最有用的事，莫过于帮助他们培养这种美德，而AI的出现使它变得更重要，而不是更不重要。实践智慧超越了对一般规则的简单了解——比如“不要撒谎”——并像某种道德机器人那样机械地应用它们。它关乎在面对生活抛给你的复杂、动态情境时知道如何做出良好判断。有时那实际上意味着违背一条经典规则（在某些情况下，你应该撒谎！）。如果你已经

当你磨练了实践智慧，你将能够辨别特定情境中具有道德意义的关键特征，并给出与该情境高度契合的回应。这正是学生们步入更广阔世界时需要擅长的思考方式。技术创新的飞速步伐意味着他们将不得不一次又一次地选择如何利用新兴技术——以及如何不去利用。他们现在能获得的最佳训练，就是如何明智地做出这类选择。不幸的是，课堂上使用生成式AI恰恰可能会破坏这一点，因为它移除了一种极其宝贵的东西：摩擦。遭遇摩擦是我们锻炼认知肌肉的方式。将其从画面中移除，短期内会让事情变得更容易，但从长远来看，可能导致智力上的技能退化，我们的认知肌肉因缺乏使用而逐渐减弱。“实践智慧就像其他所有美德一样，通过实践来积累，所以如果你没有机会推理，也没有机会练习对某些事情进行深思，你以后就无法很好地深思，”技术哲学家香农·瓦洛去年告诉我。“我们需要大量认知锻炼来发展并保持实践智慧。有理由担心认知自动化会剥夺我们建立和保持这些认知肌肉的机会。”那么，你如何帮助学生保持并增强他们的实践智慧呢？通过尽可能多地给他们练习深思和选择的机会，将摩擦重新引入。如果我来设计课程，我不会采用严格的“禁止AI”政策。相反，我会对学生坦诚人文学科的真实益处，并解释为何盲目地利用AI作弊就是剥夺自己获得这种益处。然后，在写论文时，我会给他们两个选择：他们可以在AI帮助下写作，或者不依赖AI。两者完全可以。但如果他们确实从AI获得帮助，他们还必须写一篇课堂反思文章，解释为什么选择使用聊天机器人，以及他们认为这如何改变了他们的思维和学习过程。我会让它比原始作业更短，但比一段更长，这样迫使他们发展出他们试图避免使用的推理技能。作为助教，你可以向教授提出这个建议，但他们可能不会采纳。不幸的是，你在这里的自主权有限（除非你愿意冒险失去工作或离开它）。在这种情况下，你所能做的就是行使你确实拥有的自主权。所以，充分利用每一分。既然你带领讨论课，你处于有利位置来引导你的学生。

来锻炼他们在对话中的认知能力。你甚至可以组织一场关于AI的辩论：让一半学生为使用聊天机器人写论文辩护，另一半则反对。如果教授坚持严格的“禁止AI”政策，而你遇到明显由AI撰写的文章，你可能别无选择，只能举报。但如果某篇文章存在疑点，而学生在讨论中表现出非常深入的思考，你或许应倾向于宽容处理。至少这样你知道他们实现了最重要的目标。这一切都不容易。我对你以及所有在这个混乱环境中挣扎的教育者深表同情。事实上，如果有些教育者正遭受道德伤害——即当你感到被迫违背自身价值观时产生的心理状态——我也不会感到惊讶。但或许可以安慰你的是，记住这件事远非你一人所能左右。生成式AI对当前形式的人文学科教育构成了生存威胁。未来几年，人文学科部门必须经历范式转变，否则将消亡。如果他们想生存，就需要对自己真正的使命进行残酷的诚实审视。目前，从你处于范式转变前的视角来看，你所能做的只是做出留给你的选择。

我回想起了Shannon Vallor的第一本书《技术与美德：值得向往未来的哲学指南》。如果有一本书能让AI世界中的每个人都读到，那非它莫属。我认为它对其他人同样有益，因为我们都需培养Vallor所称的“技术道德美德”——这些特质能让我们很好地适应新兴技术。《纽约客》上一篇关于AI与认知萎缩的文章让我找到了一篇2024年的心理学论文，题为《思考的不愉快：心理努力与负面情绪关联的元分析综述》。作者的结论是：“我们建议，心理努力本质上令人厌恶。”再说一遍？是的，有时我只想关掉大脑看Netflix，但有时思考一个挑战性话题却如此愉快！对我来说，这就像跑步或举重：太多会令人疲惫，但适量则令人振奋。而“适量”的感觉会随着我的练习多少而上下波动。天体生物学家Sara Imari Walker在《Noema》杂志上发表了一篇题为《AI是生命》的文章，颇具挑衅性。她提醒我们，进化产生了我们，而我们产生了AI。“因此，它属于与生命起源同时出现的远古信息谱系的一部分，”她写道，“技术并非人为地替代生命——它就是生命。”需要明确的是，她并非主张技术是活的；她是在说技术是人类生命的延伸。

ife，作为我们自身物种的延伸。这个故事最初发表于《The Highlight》，Vox会员专属杂志。要每月抢先获取会员专属故事，请立即加入Vox会员计划。查看更多：建议教育未来完美政策The Highlight你的里程可能不同如何为孩子们准备应对AI对就业市场的颠覆？作者：西格尔·塞缪尔在AI时代寻找工作意义的指南作者：西格尔·塞缪尔OpenAI与五角大楼交易后，每个人都应提出的一个问题作者：西格尔·塞缪尔用最新的Vox填字游戏放松大脑支持屠宰美国野马的最大倡导者可能出乎你意料一位福音派人士解释人们对她的信仰有何误解Z世代的政见并非人们所想播客一个人制作了深度伪造应用，将女性照片转为裸体，结果并不顺利电子邮件（必填）注册提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: Why you never really get over high school
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Popularity, one of the defining fixations of adolescence, seems to be seared into our consciousness for decades after we leave school. Before I was friends with Georgia*, I was scared of her.  One incident sticks in my mind. We were 14, and my best friend at the time was throwing a party – the kind that takes place in a rented church hall and where practically the whole school year turns up. But there was one group of people that my friend had neglected to invite. Georgia and her posse strode towards us across the playground, observers turning to stare. She was a terrifying bolt of fake tan, peroxide hair extensions and luminous sportswear – what could she possibly want with the likes of us? We froze as she came to a halt.  "We're invited to your party, yeah?" Georgia demanded of my friend. "Yes, of course," my friend managed to stutter back. Satisfied, Georgia turned on her heel and marched away. Another girl nearby murmured, "You don't have to invite them if you don't want to." But we all knew that yes, yes she did. You probably have similar high school recollections – of finding yourself at the sharp end of playground politics. Maybe you have memories of your own Georgia, a popular kid who could induce fear at a glance. Maybe you were a Georgia yourself. Either way, you probably remember it well. After speaking to hundreds of people about their experiences of high school, Mitch Prinstein, a professor of psychology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in the US, found that people's memories of those who once ruled over the school corridors – the queen bees, the prom kings, the star athletes – were remarkably potent. We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through – Mitch Prinstein Even decades after leaving school, most people are able to effortlessly recall the name of the most popular kid in their year – more so than the names of teachers and other classmates, wrote Prinstein ​i​n his 2017 book Popular: The Power of Likability in a Status-Obsessed World . And it's not just the memories that stick. We might be inclined to think that the high school hierarchy becomes irrelevant once we step beyond the school gates for the last time. But it turns out that it can exert a strange and persistent hold over us.  Research shows that how popular and well-liked we were as teenagers can influence our lives for years to come in everything from how we make sense of our social interactions to the strength of our romantic relations, our life satisfaction and even our health.  It was American psychologist John Coie who changed the way researchers thought about popularity.  His now-seminal studies in the early 1980s began by asking school kids two simple questions about their classmates: Who do you like the most? Who do you like the least? In the childish handwriting scrawled across hundreds of scraps of paper, Coie would trace new insights about human social behaviour.  You might think that children would be either broadly liked or disliked by their peers. In fact, Coie and his colleagues found kids can be both liked and disliked by different students, or neither liked nor disliked. Some children were named a lot by their peers – they were highly visible, like tiny celebrities. Others were barely mentioned at all. For the first time, Coie used the kids' answers to propose five social categories. "Accepted" and "rejected" for those who were widely liked or disliked respectively. "Controversial" for those who got a high number of both "likes" and "dislikes". "Neglected" for those who were hardly mentioned either way. And "average", for kids who weren't too extreme in any one direction (though most leaned towards one of the categories). Many studies have confirmed the usefulness of these labels. They generally find that about 40% of kids are "average" and 60% fit into one of the remaining four categories.  The most liked kids tend to be seen by their peers as kind, encouraging and supportive, while "neglecteds" tend to be quiet and withdrawn. "Rejected" kids are likely to be either aggressive and to bully others, or unassertive, socially anxious and the victims of bullying themselves . "Controversials", the rarest group, split the crowd – they're typically seen as class clowns or rebels. Remarkably, Coie found that children's labels largely stayed the same when they were introduced to new peer groups. And while the initial research was on primary school kids, many studies have replicated the findings in adolescents. One found that around half of kids maintain the same label they had at primary school five years later in high school.  "I'd had such a bad experience in primary school, and I always remember my mum saying 'It'll be better when you go to high school'," says Connie*, another friend I've asked about her high school experience. "But I think once you've been bullied, or if you have something that makes you visibly different… it was like I was easy pickings."  After being targeted by bullies in the first few months of high school, for reasons including being mixed race at a predominantly white institution, Connie switched schools. At her new school however, she soon encountered a similar pattern. (Read about the powerful new ways being discovered to fight bullying .) While the labels stay the same, the social dynamics shift dramatically between primary school and high school. In primary school, the "popular" kids are simply those who are best liked – often those who are well-behaved and excel at school, because at that point, kids values typically align with their adult supervisors. At high school, that changes . Adults and everything they stand for become woefully undesirable. A conscientious over-achiever might find themselves relegated to "nerd" status, while a rowdier, more divisive kid might find their star unexpectedly in ascendance. On the phone to the one-time playground terror and my now close friend Georgia, I ask her if she considered herself popular at high school. She tells me she didn't think of herself in this way. "'Popular' makes it sound as if people like you and I don't think we were necessarily liked," she says. "Maybe it was a bit more like, infamous… loud and attention-seeking." As a young teen, Georgia embodied the "controversial" archetype. She acted out aggressively and was disruptive in class. For all those who loved her, there were probably a fair few who didn't. I tell her that people, including myself, were pretty scared of her at one point. But she's wrong about this making her ineligible for the "popular" label.  "We start paying attention to who might be getting the most attention, who might be more dominant or 'cool'," says Prinstein. "Those who start becoming more physically attractive, those who are fitting into peer norms, [like] those who dress well or are good at sports."  Engaging in "pseudomature" behaviour – actions associated with older teens or adults – is another fast track to status. Teens who drink alcohol, take drugs and engage in precocious romantic behaviour are more likely to be considered popular – at least for a time. At around age 15, this behaviour stops conferring status to the same degree.  As high schoolers begin to mature, overt status-seeking becomes less socially expedient, and "likeability" begins to reassert itself as an important determinant of social standing. But the ripple effects from these early experiences in extreme social stratification can be consequential. "The experiences that we're having as kids – whether we're well liked, whether we're popular or high status – seem to have an enduring effect on us even 40 years later," says Prinstein. "Likability and status have pretty opposite effects. Likability is good. It generally leads to all kinds of positive health, work, academic and psychological outcomes.  "High status actually leads to the opposite ." Researchers used to think of high school culture as an immature version of adult society. In the 1960s, they began to understand that this "peer culture" was something much stranger – a parallel world animated by its own quixotic fascinations and sets of codes.  Rather than a simple hierarchy, the high school social landscape features a dynamic system of cliques. The key archetypes recur across popular culture, from American Pie to The Breakfast Club : the populars, the burnouts, the rejects and the nerds.  For the first few years of high school, the boundaries between cliques tend to be rigid. "Young people can become remarkably clannish, intolerant and cruel in their exclusion of others who are 'different'," wrote German-American psychoanalyst Erik Erikson in his 1959 book , Identity and the Life Cycle. It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence – Lucy Foulkes This intolerance, Erikson contended, might be "a necessary defence" against the loss of the identity one had as a child, combined with a mystifying onslaught of hormonal changes, and the overwhelming nature of the future, with all its possibilities and choices. Adolescents help each other through this discomfort "by forming cliques and stereotyping themselves", he suggested. This self-sorting makes it easier for teenagers to navigate their social worlds, because each person's relative "category" dictates how they should be treated.   One thing that is overlooked in popular culture, however, is the large swathe of teens who don't subscribe to any particular subculture. A 1985 study found that about 45% of highschoolers defined themselves simply as "normal". While the popular kids claimed they were all about looking good and partying, self-defined "normals" said things like "I'm just a regular teen". Being "abnormal" and standing out for the wrong reasons can be socially catastrophic. Connie remembers arriving at her new school aged 13 and finding it impossible to gain a foothold on the slippery social edifice. She describes her attempts to amplify different parts of herself in search of the right clique.   "I remember trying to be friends with the nerdy girls. I remember trying to be friends with the cool girls," she says. "I'd be like, 'Oh, I'm really bookish, I do all my homework.' And then that wasn't working, so it was like, 'Oh, I wear makeup, I do my hair,' that sort of thing. I tried to fit in with the music people. I started playing the trumpet."  But it was to no avail. "I think I knew in my heart that it just wasn't working," she says. "There was nowhere for me to slot in. By the end, I was just completely ignored by everyone."  Towards the end of high school, the punishing social hierarchy relaxes a little.  In the early 1990s, researcher David Kinney carried out an ethnographic research project where he embedded himself in a high school to observe the shifting boundaries of cliques up close. He tracked former "nerds" who managed to transition to "normals".  The rigidity of early high school cliques might reflect the limited cognitive capacities of young adolescents, he noted . While young teens are increasingly able to self-reflect, many are unable to differentiate between how often they think about themselves (a lot) and how often others do.  For many of the young "nerds" Kinney spoke to, this resulted in a debilitating self-focus and paralysis in social interactions. Eventually, continued cognitive development meant that former nerds were able to feel less fearful, and to surround themselves with peers who provided positive feedback. As teens mature, the strictures of conformity begin to loosen. Popular kids might even face threats from alternative, rebellious types. Kinney's study found that in later years, the "trendies" were challenged by students with "outrageous appearance and rowdy behaviour", who "competed with them for schoolwide popularity".  Some of these subtle shifts must have been underway when, aged 15, Georgia first asked me to hang out with her, but I still remember experiencing confusion and disbelief. At that point, I was a member of a predominantly male group of stoners. Was Georgia trying to play some kind of practical joke on me? Would I be lured out only to be humiliated in some way?   Almost 20 years later, I ask Georgia why she wanted to befriend me, something I've never asked her before. I'm wondering which of my sparkling attributes might have attracted her attention – my wit, my charm? "I guess there was a weirdness that we all shared," she says hesitantly. "Like, none of us were normal."  Given all its unique quirks, it’s remarkable how often we use high school as a frame of reference for adult interactions. When Lucy Foulkes, a psychologist at the University of Oxford in the UK and author of Coming of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Us , shared a social media post about the "mean girl" effect, she was met with an outpouring of recognition. "A lot of people were saying, it's not just teenagers, I see this in the workplace… I see this with mums at the school gate," says Foulkes. "It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence."  Foulkes points out that teens are surrounded by the same people almost every day for years in a way "that just doesn't really happen in adulthood, other than in the army or in prison. There is an intensity from the environment that goes beyond what's happening inside their brains." It's this intensity that partly explains why these experiences stay lodged within us, says Prinstein, shaping how we make sense of social encounters for years to come.  "We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through," says Prinstein. He points to studies suggesting that the mental model we use to process our social worlds begins to form in childhood , and that the memory-processing parts of the brain are active when people think about social behaviour . "Those memories are being brought back out all the time."  Many of us have likely wondered what happened to the "cool kids" we knew as teens. In a 2015 study , Joseph Allen, a professor of psychology at the University of Virginia in the US, sought to find out. His discoveries did not bode well for once-popular youths. Following 184 adolescents in the south-eastern US from ages 13 to 23, Allen found that status-hungry young people who engaged in pseudomature behaviour in their early teens were at greater risk of long-term difficulties in close relationships and criminal behaviour.  An early taste for alcohol and drugs was tied to greater vulnerability to substance abuse and addiction issues later in life. And a focus on status at an early age led to shallower bonds and difficulties sustaining friendships and romantic relationships.  The experience of being rejected can also leave scars. Prinstein's research found that rejected high school students were likely to become more depressed over time . He hypothesised that a negative feedback loop was at play, where the experience of rejection begets more withdrawal, which in turn intensifies feelings of rejection. People can absolutely turn it around. The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – Mitch Prinstein By contrast, "likeability" – being "accepted" – in high school and generally, is one of the strongest predictors for positive life outcomes like a successful career , good health and strong relationships , even over and above factors like intelligence and socioeconomic background. Still, people who experience rejection can also develop important strengths, such as becoming more adept at identifying how others are feeling or being more aware of others being mistreated . Such emotional intelligence has been shown to be helpful in navigating personal relationships and the world of work .  And a child doesn't have to be "accepted" to enjoy a fulfilling social life as an adult. Studies have found that even just having one or two good friends as a teenager can confer a protective effect and strengthen future relationships.   Most importantly, it's within our power to change how our early experiences affect us. According to Prinstein, the high-school-honed social scripts we approach interactions with can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. "When we enter into a social context, we may be focusing on those pieces of information that confirm our worst expectations," he says. "Then we will behave in ways that might actually encourage more negative experiences." By choosing to update these frameworks – for example, deciding that a peer's ambiguous comment was probably not intended to upset us – we can help ourselves to have more rewarding experiences, he says.  As a reformed "high status" teen who engaged in risky, pseudomature behaviour from a young age, Georgia says, "I kind of have a sadness for my younger self, that I never got to experience just being a normal kid." She tells me that an early experience of seeing a friend beaten up, combined with abusive behaviour at home, convinced her to act aggressively to project invulnerability.  More like this: • The perks and pitfalls of laughing at yourself • How much of our personalities are determined at birth? • How I changed my personality in six weeks   She laments the fact that she didn't get more support at that age and was instead typecast by teachers as a "bad kid". "It's completely shaped my career trajectory and my fierce advocacy for vulnerable people," she says. Connie, meanwhile, says her early experiences of rejection eventually fed into a pattern of self-sabotage. "I think I'd given up on myself in a lot of ways, and I had so many self-destructive behaviours that it then became hard to maintain friendships," she says. This culminated in a period of crisis in her late adolescence, which she has since worked hard to heal from. More than a decade on, she has figured out what she loves – including a creative practice and a fulfilling career – and says she rarely thinks about her high school days.  Both Connie and Georgia are testament to the fact that the labels we once wore in high school don't have to be a life sentence.  "People can absolutely turn it around," Prinstein concurs. "The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – meaning we are more likely to repeat our patterns."  * Names have been changed. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter   by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
